Situation1: Your friend has misunderstood the tone of your text message and replied sounding hurt. You need to call them right now to explain.
Expectation2: Arrive at the polling station during designated voting hours
Situation2: Late-afternoon errands leave just a couple of hours before the polls close.
Story: I glance at my phone and see the message from Jamie—her words are clipped, and I can tell she’s upset. She thinks I was annoyed with her, but it was just a rushed text. I know I should call her right now, talk it through, and clear things up before it festers. That’s what friends do: communicate, don’t let misunderstandings grow. But as I reach for my phone, I remember the polling station closes in less than two hours. I’ve already put off voting all day, and if I don’t go now, I might miss my chance. I promised myself I’d vote, that I’d do my part. My chest tightens as I picture Jamie waiting for my call, feeling hurt, while I’m standing in line at the polls. I want to be a good friend, but I also want to be a responsible citizen. The minutes are slipping away, and I can’t do both at once. My heart pounds as I weigh the expectations pressing in from both sides, torn between the friend who needs me and the duty I owe my community.
